units.name: Hesperian transition undivided unit
units.description: Irregular plateaus hundreds of kilometers across. Layered. Hundreds of meters to kilometers thick. (lat –6.41° N., long 156.42° E; lat –6.17° N., long 286.05° E.; localities 26, 28)
units.additional: In southern Elysium Planitia along highland/lowland boundary and within and east of Valles Marineris. Superposes units Nhu, Nve, mNh, and eNh; gradational with units eHt, Hve, and HNt (Hesperian part); overlain by units lHt, Ht, Hto, AHtu, Aa, and lAv. Includes hydrated sulfate spectral signatures; fluted slopes in places. Linear ridges, anabranching sinuous ridges, and wrinkle ridges common
units.interpretation: Fine-grained eolian sediments and (or) pyroclastic air-fall deposits. Modified by fluvial dissection and eolian erosion. Linear ridges and grooves form yardangs. Tectonically contracted. Channels mostly inverted. Altered by acidic weathering in places

units.name: Amazonian and Hesperian impact unit
units.description: Craters with rims and surrounding blankets; some include single to multi-lobed blanket forms, dense secondary crater chains, and (or) central peak or pit. Blanket thicknesses of meters to a few hundred meters. (lat 23.17° N., long 207.77° E.
units.additional: Global occurrence. Superposes Noachian units; other unit superposition relations diverse. High kilometer-scale surface roughness; crater floors may be smooth to rough
units.interpretation: Upturned, ejected, and brecciated target rocks and sediments, with local areas of impact melt. Post-impact mass-wasting and fluvial-lacustrine and eolian infill of craters common

source: USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3292, Geologic Map of Mars (Tanaka and others, 2014), unit polygons from the USGS-hosted ArcGIS feature service, layer 3 'Global_Geology'
citation: Tanaka, K.L., Skinner, J.A., Jr., Dohm, J.M., Irwin, R.P., III, Kolb, E.J., Fortezzo, C.M., Platz, T., Michael, G.G., and Hare, T.M., 2014, Geologic map of Mars: U.S. Geological Survey Scientific Investigations Map 3292, scale 1:20,000,000, https://doi.org/10.3133/sim3292
scale_note: This is a 1:20,000,000 map of the whole planet. At that scale one millimetre on the printed map is 20 km on the ground, and the whole walk-planner box (9.5 km by 19.6 km) is smaller than one square millimetre of it. A contact line here can be several kilometres from where the rocks really change, so this layer says only what kind of terrain the region is in the global picture: it must not be used to say what rock is under any particular step of a walk. No finer published USGS geologic map of Gale Crater or Mount Sharp exists as GIS data (checked 2026-11-14).
coordinates: longitude east-positive and planetocentric latitude in degrees on the Mars 2000 sphere (radius 3,396,190 m), as returned by the service when asked for GCS_Mars_2000_Sphere; the service itself stores a Robinson projection
rings_note: Each ring is closed (first point repeated last) and clipped to clip_box, so straight edges along the box are cuts, not contacts. ring_roles says whether a ring is an outer boundary or a hole in the source polygon; drawing all rings of a unit with the even-odd fill rule gives the right shape.
simplification: Douglas-Peucker, tolerance 0.0005 degrees (about 30 m), then rounded to 4 decimals; 3829 source vertices became 102

point_check.note: computed here from the unclipped polygons; the service's own point query gives the same unit

track_units_note: Which unit polygon each stretch of the rover track (chain_m from data/site.json) falls in, by point-in-polygon on the unclipped source polygons. Because of the map scale the changeover chain is uncertain by kilometres.
cors: The feature service answers with access-control-allow-origin: * (tested 2026-11-14), so a browser could query it live; this file is a baked copy so the app needs no network.
